explanation: Cache memory is a smaller, faster memory that sits between the CPU and main memory. It exploits spatial locality, the tendency for a program to access nearby memory locations sequentially.  By storing blocks of data (cache lines) from main memory, cache improves performance by reducing the average time to access data.  When the CPU needs data, it first checks the cache. If the data is present (a cache hit), access is fast. If not (a cache miss), the CPU retrieves the data from main memory, potentially bringing in an entire cache line to improve future access times.
syntax: No direct syntax, but concepts include cache line size, associativity (number of ways), and replacement policy (e.g., LRU). These parameters influence performance.
code_example: ; Assume a simple array access pattern exhibiting spatial locality
mov rcx, array_start ; Load the base address of the array
mov rax, [rcx + rbx*8] ; Access array element (assuming 64-bit elements)
jl loop_start ; Continue loop if more elements to process
; array_start is the start address of an array
; array_size represents the size of the array
example_explanation: This assembly code snippet demonstrates spatial locality.  Accessing array elements sequentially (using `[rcx + rbx*8]`) leads to consecutive memory locations being accessed. If the cache line size is larger than a single element, subsequent accesses are likely to be cache hits, significantly improving performance. A larger cache line size will likely result in more cache hits and faster overall execution, due to spatial locality. If the array elements were not sequentially accessed, the chances of cache misses would increase.
